headlines.title: 2 dead, 2 injured after shootings, collision within minutes in Vallejo
headlines.description: Two shootings and one car crash within minutes of each other rocked Vallejo on Tuesday morning, leaving two people dead and two others injured. At approximately 8 a.m., a man was shot in the area of Castlewood Drive and Springs Road near Vallejo’s east side. The man was taken to a hospital by emergency personnel, where he is in critical condition, according to Vallejo police. Minutes later, at 8:15 a.m., two vehicles crashed in South Vallejo in the 1000 block of Sonoma Boulevard. One driver, a man, died from his injuries at the scene. The other driver was taken to a hospital and is expected to survive. At 8:23 a.m., a man was shot in the 200 block of Marin Street, just blocks away from the crash. The man was taken to a hospital, where he died from his wounds. Police have not confirmed whether either shooting or crash are related and did not provide further identifying information about the victims or suspected shooters. All three cases are under investigation, according to a spokesperson for the Vallejo Police Department. The city’s crisis response team, called IHART, along with a chaplain and officers are canvassing the affected areas to provide resources and trauma-informed care, police said.

headlines.title: Woman killed in suspected hit-and-run collision on I-680 in San Jose
headlines.description: A woman was struck and killed in a suspected hit-and-run collision on southbound Interstate 680 in San Jose late Monday night, according to the California Highway Patrol. Officers responded around 11 p.m. to the collision involving a pedestrian reported on southbound I-680 north of North Capitol Avenue. The woman, whose name has not been released, was pronounced dead at the scene, CHP officials said. Investigators determined that a vehicle struck her and the driver then fled. No description of the vehicle or driver was immediately available. The highway reopened as of early Tuesday morning. Anyone with information about the case is asked to call the CHP’s San Jose-area office at 408-961-0900.

headlines.title: Sonoma County declares local emergency ahead of expected El Niño flooding
headlines.description: Even before the first winter storm of the year, Sonoma County is declaring a local emergency in anticipation of above-average flooding expected from this season’s El Niño weather pattern. Sonoma County leaders are preparing for above-average rainfall from December through March. The National Weather Service is predicting a 70% chance that it will be the strongest El Niño in more than 70 years. The local emergency proclamation will help the county get an early start on staffing and training. There’s also a plan for community engagement, including a focus on people living in mobile homes near the lower Russian River. County crews will also continue preventive drainage clearing and road repairs. Sonoma County isn’t alone in preparing early. Two weeks ago, Gov. Gavin Newsom declared a statewide state of emergency to coordinate preparedness. The governor requested recommendations from the state’s environmental protection and natural resources agencies by Oct. 16.

headlines.title: ‘Horses and Heroes' brings new experience to SF Fleet Week
headlines.description: A new event is bringing service members out of the city and onto horseback. The first-of-its-kind Fleet Week event, called “Heroes and Horses,” is taking place at Ocean View Stables in Daly City. A couple dozen service members are participating, with some riding horses along a trail down to the beach. The experience grew out of the passion of a veteran-turned-business owner who found healing and purpose through horsemanship after his deployment to Afghanistan. The event comes as Fleet Week gets underway in San Francisco with traditional activities including the air show and ship tours. NBC Bay Area’s Ginger Conejero Saab has the full report in the video above.

headlines.title: Stanford scientist wins a Nobel Prize, then makes school lunches for his kids
headlines.description: Dr. Karl Deisseroth spent hours fielding congratulatory calls after learning early Monday that he had won a Nobel Prize for medicine for helping to open a new field of brain science called optogenetics. But it wasn’t long before the scientist asked for a break from all the attention for a more ordinary task: He needed to make school lunches for his children, who were asleep in the family home in Stanford, where their father had been speaking in the middle of the night with journalists and well-wishers. Deisseroth, 54, shared this year’s medicine prize with two researchers in Germany for their work in optogenetics, a field that combines light with genes to switch on and off neurons in living brains. A self-described night owl, the Howard Hughes Medical Institute investigator and Stanford University professor often works past midnight. After reviewing papers and emailing his students, he said he had just gone to lie down when he got the call from the Nobel Assembly in Stockholm. “I almost felt as if I’d lost the power of forming words,” he told The Associated Press, “but I recovered after a minute or two.” He regained speech quickly enough for remote interviews with AP science reporters. Speedy emails with the Stanford communications staff had helped put them in touch. “No real sleep was achieved,” he said an hour after the announcement. As the science reporters chatted with Deisseroth over the phone and Zoom, an AP photographer and videographer raced to his home in Stanford. The photographer arrived around 3:30 a.m. to find Halloween decorations outside the home but just one light on inside. He was worried he had the wrong house before mustering the courage to knock on the door. Dr. Michelle Monje-Deisseroth, the scientist’s wife, answered and ushered the photographer into their home, where the Nobel winner was taking calls from the couch. Monje-Deisseroth, an HHMI investigator and Stanford pediatric neuro-oncologist, was at his side when she wasn’t making coffee for the Stanford communications staff who had joined the celebration. Deisseroth was surprised to hear his work had been honored with a Nobel Prize, he told the AP, but his wife was not. Deisseroth recounted the research he conducted with fellow Nobel winners Peter Hegemann and Georg Nagel, and its real-world impact. “For me, I’m a physician-scientist. I am a psychiatrist. I care about patients and my patients who have autism, who have depression,” he said. “I care about the hope that this brings. But I’m also a basic scientist, and I care about understanding this amazing organ, the brain, and how it works and how it integrates and computes and delivers all the things that make us human.” As Deisseroth wrapped up the interviews, he told the Stanford staff he needed an hourlong break beginning at 6:30 a.m. His kids would be waking up, he said, and they would need lunches before leaving for school. When one of the Stanford representatives wondered if the neighbors would mind all the late-night commotion, Monje-Deisseroth shrugged it off. They live in faculty housing, she said. There are a lot of Nobels in the neighborhood. __ Ramakrishnan reported from New York. Associated Press writers Stefanie Dazio in Berlin and Lauran Neergaard in Washington contributed to this report. ___ AP Nobel Prizes: https://apnews.com/hub/nobel-prizes
headlines.source: Noah Berger | The Associated Press, Terry Chea | The Associated Press and Adithi Ramakrishnan | The Associated Press

headlines.title: Berkeley candidates rally against surveillance technology
headlines.description: A group of candidates running for Berkeley City Council came together Tuesday morning to rally against surveillance technology outside City Hall. The seven candidates are opposing a City Council proposal involving license plate-reading cameras, drones and other surveillance technology. The candidates also say they are pledging to vote against mass surveillance and to remove the city’s Flock cameras. The candidates were joined by the former chair of the Police Accountability Board, which formally opposed the technology in 2023.

headlines.title: 1 dead in crash on Highway 92 in San Mateo
headlines.description: At least one person was killed early Tuesday morning on westbound state Route 92 in San Mateo after a vehicle collision, according to the California Highway Patrol. The collision was reported at about 6:10 a.m. The CHP later issued a Sig Alert for westbound Route 92 east of U.S. Highway 101 due to lanes blocked by the crash. By 7:35 a.m., the affected lanes were reopened. The CHP did not immediately provide further information about the fatal collision.

headlines.title: Oakland City Council to vote on 45-day data center moratorium
headlines.description: The Oakland City Council is expected to vote Tuesday on a 45-day moratorium on new data centers amid concerns about noise and impacts on the electrical grid and water systems. A number of Oakland residents are concerned that new data centers could be too noisy and strain the city’s electrical grid and water systems, similar to concerns raised in other parts of the Bay Area and across the country. Oakland is specifically concerned about plans for a 20,000-square-foot building downtown. The project could provide computing power for artificial intelligence and robotics. The developer calls it an “innovation center.” Some Oakland residents have expressed support for data centers because they could bring new jobs and revenue to the city. Nearby Richmond and Gilroy recently approved their own 45-day moratoriums. In San Francisco, a proposal to prohibit data centers for 45 days is also being considered. Oakland’s City Council meeting is scheduled to begin at 3:30 p.m. Tuesday.

headlines.title: Oakland police investigate early-morning shooting on Rilea Way
headlines.description: The Oakland Police Department is investigating an early-morning shooting that left a victim hospitalized Sunday. Officers responded to a report of a shooting just after 2:30 a.m. in the 4300 block of Rilea Way. Upon arrival, officers located a victim suffering from an apparent gunshot wound, according to the Oakland Police Department. The victim was transported to a hospital and was last reported in stable condition. According to a preliminary investigation, the suspect allegedly assaulted the victim and pointed a firearm at them. As the victim raised an arm to defend themselves, they were shot. The suspect then allegedly pistol-whipped the victim before fleeing on foot. The identities of the parties involved were not immediately available. The investigation is ongoing. Authorities ask anyone with information to contact the Felony Assault Unit at 510-238-3426 or via email at cidvideos@oaklandca.gov.

headlines.title: Multi-agency drug bust dismantles large-scale meth lab in Central Valley desert
headlines.description: Federal and local law enforcement agencies have successfully dismantled a large-scale clandestine methamphetamine conversion lab housed inside a residence in a rural desert neighborhood in the Central Valley, the Drug Enforcement Administration’s San Francisco Division announced Monday. The operation was led by DEA San Francisco agents in coordination with the Kern County Sheriff’s Office and the San Bernardino County Sheriff’s Department following an intensive narcotics investigation. Due to the extreme hazards posed by large quantities of hazardous, unknown chemicals inside the residence, on-site lab personnel were assisted by the San Bernardino County Fire Department’s Hazmat unit to safely process the dangerous and unsanitary facility. The bust yielded major seizures and arrests, including: — Five suspects arrested from Sinaloa, Mexico. — 574 pounds of methamphetamine seized. — 1,567 pounds of methamphetamine in solution seized. — Three firearms seized. — Several thousand dollars in U.S. currency seized.

headlines.title: Oakland's Children's Fairyland receives $5M state investment for historic park upgrades
headlines.description: Children’s Fairyland in Oakland is receiving a $5 million state investment to ensure the nearly 80-year-old storybook park can preserve its magic for generations to come. For generations of Bay Area families, Children’s Fairyland has been a place where fairy tales, play, and imagination come to life. The funding comes directly from the state budget and completes the first phase of the park’s long-term capital plan. “This is such an iconic piece of Oakland,” said Kymberly Miller, CEO of Children’s Fairyland. “It is a huge part of what being an Oaklander is and an East Bay icon, so this is real for us. It is giving us what we need to make the future.” Of the total funding, $2 million will support operations, while another $3 million will fund restoration and upgrades, including replacing 100-year-old pipes. “A foundational beginning,” Miller said. “We have a long way to go, we have to improve the physical space of the park, which means maintenance of sets, maybe some new buildings so we can have indoor programming during the winter.” Fairyland celebrated 75 years in Oakland last year. Its storybook world made it a pioneer in children’s entertainment, though the park has also weathered major challenges, including the pandemic. Oakland Mayor Barbara Lee emphasized that the investment ensures families will continue having a place to play and make memories. “It’s vital funding that we need right here in Oakland,” Mayor Lee said, adding, “It’s really a storybook that comes to life. And so regardless of how old you are or how young you are, my family can attest to the fact. This is a dream come true.” In a statement, Assemblymember Mia Bonta said she is proud to deliver real funding wins that preserve the artistic and cultural legacy of Oakland. Miller noted that the support represents a broader endorsement of the park’s mission: “I think our local leaders and Governor Newsom have given Fairyland a vote of confidence. The time is now to come close to Fairyland, get involved whether it is volunteering your time or energy or your treasure to make sure we last the next 76 years.”

headlines.title: Santa Clara County kicks off early voting, mail-in ballots amid heightened security focus
headlines.description: Early voting officially got underway in Santa Clara County as election officials began mailing out more than 1 million ballots to voters ahead of the Nov. 3 election. The Santa Clara County Registrar of Voters also marked the milestone by hosting a media day in conjunction with the county sheriff to address election security and integrity. The proactive messaging comes in response to repeated, unproven claims by President Trump accusing California of “rigging” elections. At the registrar’s office on Berger Drive in San Jose, in-person voting is now open, complemented by about 100 drop boxes set up throughout the county. While some voters remain unfazed by the rhetoric, others noted that the national conversation influenced how they chose to cast their ballots. “I have complete trust in the election system,” said San Jose voter May Lee. “I don’t have any concerns about in-person versus mail-in voting. I personally always go in-person because I feel like I want to ‘engage’ actively in the process and go on the day to vote.” Another San Jose voter, Marina Moreno, said political controversy motivated her to vote in person rather than risking mail-in options. “Right now because of what Trump is going through… saying that he can push votes and stuff like that, I don’t want that to happen to my vote,” Moreno said. When asked if she feared presidential interference rather than a rigged election, she replied, “Yes.” To combat potential disruptions and reassure the public, the registrar has coordinated closely with law enforcement. County officials outlined various safety measures, including low-key patrols by sheriff’s deputies at voting locations. “It could be protesters, electioneering, anything like that, so we do work closely to have a variety of contingency plans in place,” said Matt Moreles of the Registrar of Voters. “We are doing everything we can here at the County to ensure that everybody has a safe and secure experience at the voting locations and that voters can cast their ballots free from any intimidation or interference.” California Attorney General Rob Bonta echoed those commitments, noting that the state is prepared to deploy election observers if needed, just as it did during previous elections when federal monitors were present, to ensure voters feel safe and laws are followed. Registrar voting booths in San Jose on Berger Drive are open during normal business hours from 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., with additional in-person voting centers slated to open across the county on Oct. 24.
